awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: Massive, empirical, scalable generation of small molecule and protein interaction data to enable the discovery of medicines at scale with machine learning
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project will be to enable the discovery of new medicines at an unprecedented rate, by empowering researchers across the globe to launch discovery programs in weeks at a dramatically reduced entry price. This is in contrast to the status quo of launching a drug discovery program, which costs hundreds of thousands of dollars, requires expensive company resources, and several months of time prior to an initial readout on progress.  The outcome of this new ability may be an increased number of therapeutics that are able to make it through clinical trials and ultimately to patients.  The innovation could provide data of interactions between billions of unique small molecules and the entire human proteome. This could enable the creation of sophisticated and predictive machine learning based models to predict novel interactions between small molecules and protein sequences.  The validation and expansion of this approach would allow for continuous improvement of the ability to predict new medicines for emerging diseases. 

The proposed project will seek to demonstrate the ability to encapsulate proteins and small molecules in millions of molecular barcoded pico-scale compartments and identify the specific interactions between the proteins and small molecules contained within each of them.  The Intellectual Merit of the activity is in the construction of the materials and methods that enable this capability, which reduces the cost of a single protein and small molecule library screen by over 100X.  Current methodologies are limited to screening in much larger formats, leading to higher costs, limited parallelization, and large quantities of material required for the screen to be used.  In contrast, the innovation herein could allow for a dramatic reduction in the amount of materials required, enabling the screening of proteins in high parallelization through miniaturization, and consequently reducing cost and time required to generate a comparable sized dataset by orders of magnitude.  The project goals will be to (1) determine with control systems the ability to identify known interactions in the pico-scale format, (2) determine if non-control protein interactions are able to be identified in at 10-plex format, (3) and to determine if protein selective molecules are able to be identified in a single screen.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The discovery of new small-molecule medicines often begins by testing whether molecules can bind to proteins involved in disease. Many screening methods test one protein at a time, making broad exploration expensive and slow. Results generated in separate experiments can also be difficult to compare, combine, and reuse, limiting how much each experiment contributes to future discovery efforts. Om’s Phase I SBIR project sought to demonstrate a new screening approach that could evaluate multiple proteins in parallel using DNA-encoded libraries, in which each small molecule carries an identifying DNA tag. The central challenge was to preserve a reliable record of both the protein and the molecule involved in each potential interaction while many proteins and molecules were processed together.

The project addressed three linked technical goals. The first goal was to construct encoded protein particles that carried enough protein and identifying material to support measurable screening. Om established quantitative measurement methods and used them to evaluate key steps in particle construction and molecular capture. The team demonstrated controlled formation of the DNA-based readout and showed that a model DNA-tagged molecule could be captured and measured in the particle-based system. These results established that the core materials could be quantified and that protein-bearing particles could provide a detectable foundation for the later stages of the multiplexed workflow. 

The second goal was to preserve the association between protein identity and small-molecule identity during shared processing. Om developed a workflow in which individual protein-bearing particles and associated DNA-tagged molecules were compartmentalized in small droplets. The team demonstrated that the required DNA-processing chemistry remained active under droplet-processing conditions and that identifying information could be transferred into a sequencing-readable construct. Control experiments tested whether the expected protein and molecule identifiers remained correctly paired rather than becoming mixed or reassigned. Additional “fingerprint” experiments used deliberately designed patterns of DNA tags to test whether graded concentrations and digital presence-or-absence patterns could be recovered after processing. The intended digital patterns accounted for more than 93 percent of the relevant sequencing observations in the tested protein channels. Together, these experiments showed that the workflow could preserve designed identity patterns and provided measurable controls for detecting errors or background.

The third goal was to demonstrate an integrated multiplexed screen and determine whether the resulting sequencing data contained protein-dependent behavior. Om advanced the workflow into an experiment that evaluated 21 proteins in parallel, exceeding the 10-protein proof-of-concept scale proposed in the original Phase I plan. The experiment included negative controls, empty identifiers, sequencing quality checks, and comparisons with retained single-protein reference experiments. The resulting data were processed from sequencing reads into molecule-by-protein summaries using a defined analysis workflow. Comparisons with the reference experiments recovered protein- and construct-dependent patterns, and representative molecules showed stronger signals in their intended protein channels than in average background channels. These results demonstrate the feasibility of executing and interpreting a multiplexed screen. They are sequencing-based proof-of-concept evidence and are not presented as independently validated discoveries of new binding molecules.

Across the three goals, the Phase I project reduced the principal technical risks identified in the original proposal: producing measurable protein-bearing particles, forming the combined DNA readout, maintaining the relevant chemistry during droplet processing, preserving protein and molecule identities, and interpreting results when multiple proteins are screened together. The work also identified important controls and development needs for future studies, including capture efficiency, sequencing quality, balanced representation of protein and molecule identifiers, experimental replication, reproducibility across runs, prospective criteria for selecting promising molecules, and confirmation through independent laboratory assays.

The intellectual merit of the project lies in demonstrating a practical method for retaining protein–molecule identity in a shared experimental workflow. Instead of treating each protein screen as an isolated experiment, the approach creates a common measurement framework in which many protein contexts can be evaluated and compared. This may also produce more consistent datasets for computational analysis because the data are generated through a shared process with common controls.

The project’s broader potential impact is to make early small-molecule discovery more efficient and informative. If the method is successfully scaled and independently validated, screening multiple proteins in one workflow could reduce the cost and material required per protein, broaden the range of disease-relevant proteins that researchers can explore, and help preserve experimental results in reusable datasets. Larger and more consistent protein–molecule datasets could support pharmaceutical and biotechnology research, academic discovery programs, and future computational methods intended to learn from prior experiments. Phase I established the technical foundation for that continued development while defining the validation and quality standards required before the approach can be used for larger-scale discovery.

Importantly, the platform is intended to enable proteome-wide screening through a workflow projected to reduce cost per data point >20-fold.  The resulting datasets could power next generation machine learning models to accelerate the discovery of new medicines at scale.
